critique.reason:
The proposed $3,000 credit overstates what the contract allows, for three reasons.

1. Cap. MSA-NW-2025 §4.2 caps service credits at $1,000 in any calendar month. Even the customer's own arithmetic (six hours at 0.5% of the $100,000 fee per hour, which is $500 per hour) comes to $3,000, which exceeds the cap. The most that can be credited is $1,000.

2. Commitment threshold. §4.1 commits to 99.9% monthly availability. Over a 30-day September (720 hours), that permits about 0.72 hours (43 minutes) of unavailability. TCK-881 records 6h15m (02:10 to 08:25 UTC on 2026-09-14), so about 5.53 hours fall beyond the commitment, which is 5 full hours. Credits under §4.2 accrue only for full hours beyond the commitment, so the contractual base is 5 × $500 = $2,500, which the cap reduces to $1,000. The customer's six-hour figure ignores the commitment threshold. The cap binds whenever there are at least two full hours beyond the commitment, so $1,000 holds under any reasonable reading of the outage record.

3. Set-off. §7.4 bars withholding or set-off except for a §4.2 credit. The customer's $3,000 deduction (CRM-2207) is therefore improper beyond the $1,000 credit. The customer's written request was made within 30 days, so the credit itself is valid.

Consequence: issue a $1,000 credit memo against INV-1001. The invoice is $100,000 and the payment of $97,000 (PAY-5501) leaves a $2,000 shortfall after the credit, so the net balance is $1,000 after the credit memo and the $2,000 short-pay remains owed. Net 30 from 2026-09-01 made the due date 2026-10-01, so the balance is now past due and may accrue 1% per month under §3.2. CRM-2210 says to "follow the contract," which supports this result.

Assumption: no other unavailability occurred in September. Any additional outage would only increase the credit, and the $1,000 cap would still apply.
